title: AQA GCSE Physics · Motion and Newton’s Laws

items.stem: Which pair contains only scalar quantities?

options.text: Speed and velocity, as both describe how fast it goes
Distance and displacement, as both are lengths in metres
Distance and speed, as neither has a direction
Displacement and velocity, both having a size

items.why: Distance is how far an object moves and speed is how fast it moves; neither involves direction, so both are scalars.

items.stem: Which quantity is only fully described when a direction is given as well as a number and a unit?

options.text: Distance, measured along the path
The time taken, measured in seconds
Speed, measured in metres per second
Displacement, a vector quantity

items.why: Displacement is a vector: it is the straight-line distance from start to finish together with the direction of that line, so both parts must be stated.

items.stem: Which list gives factors that affect the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle?

options.text: Fitness alone, as everybody else walks at 1.5 m/s
Terrain and distance only, as age has no effect on it
Age, fitness, terrain and the distance travelled
Only terrain, since a person's speed is fixed

items.why: The specification lists age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled among the many factors affecting the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle.

items.stem: Which is the best estimate of the typical speed of a person walking?

options.text: 6.0 m/s, close to 22 km/h
15 m/s, or roughly 54 km/h
0.15 m/s, or about 0.5 km/h
1.5 m/s, or about 5 km/h

items.why: The specification gives walking as about 1.5 m/s, which is roughly 5 km/h - a familiar walking pace.

items.stem: A student is asked to use typical values for the speeds of a runner and a cyclist. Which pair should she use?

options.text: Running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s
Running about 6 m/s, cycling about 3 m/s
Running near 3 m/s, cycling near 3 m/s
Running 1.5 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s

items.why: The specification gives running as about 3 m/s and cycling as about 6 m/s, roughly double the running value.

items.stem: Which is the most sensible typical speed to quote for a car travelling along a motorway?

options.text: About 300 m/s, which is close to the speed of sound
About 30 m/s, which is roughly 70 miles per hour
About 10 m/s, a little faster than a cyclist
About 3 m/s, about a person's running pace

items.why: A motorway speed of about 30 m/s is close to 70 mph and is the usual typical value quoted for a car.

items.stem: Which statement about the speed of sound in air is correct?

options.text: It is fixed at 300 000 000 m/s in every case
It is always exactly 330 m/s, whatever the air
It varies, but a typical value is 330 m/s
It varies, but a typical value is 33 m/s

items.why: The specification gives a typical value of 330 m/s and notes that the speed of sound, like the speed of the wind, varies.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the velocity of a moving object?

options.text: Speed in a given direction
Simply another word for speed
How far it travels each second
How quickly its direction changes

items.why: The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, which makes velocity a vector quantity.

items.stem: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph tell you about the object?

options.text: The acceleration at that time
The distance moved so far
The total time of the trip
The speed at that moment

items.why: The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: change in distance divided by change in time.

items.stem: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph give?

options.text: The distance it has travelled
The speed it has at that moment
The average velocity so far
The object's acceleration

items.why: The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph.

items.stem: A ball is dropped near the Earth's surface. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration as it falls?

options.text: About 9.8 m/s^2 if the ball is heavy
About 9.8 m/s, growing as the ball falls
About 9.8 m/s^2, directed downwards
Zero, as it falls at steady speed

items.why: Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.

items.stem: Why is the speed of a car driven across a busy town rarely constant?

options.text: Cars are built to hold a single steady speed once moving
The driver keeps changing speed at junctions and bends
Speed can only change when the direction changes too
A speedometer shows the average speed of the trip

items.why: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.

items.stem: Which statement correctly classifies distance, displacement, speed and velocity?

options.text: Distance and displacement are scalars, with the others vectors
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors
Distance and velocity are scalars, displacement and speed vectors
All four are vectors, since each one has a size and a unit

items.why: Distance and speed carry no direction, so they are scalars; displacement and velocity each include a direction, so they are vectors.

items.stem: A car is driven round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Which statement about its motion is correct?

options.text: Both its speed and its velocity stay constant all round
Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing
Its speed is constant but its velocity keeps changing
Neither its speed nor its velocity is constant

items.why: Motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity, because the direction of motion changes continuously.

items.stem: A skydiver falling through the air reaches terminal velocity. Which statement describes what is happening?

options.text: Gravity has stopped acting, so no force acts at all now
The skydiver slows down and stops falling in the air
The air resistance is now larger than the skydiver's weight
The resultant force is zero, so velocity is steady

items.why: The drag force grows as the skydiver speeds up until it balances the weight; with zero resultant force the velocity stays constant.

items.stem: A student walks 30 m due east along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to the point where she started. What are the distance she has travelled and her displacement?

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement zero, as she ends where she began
Distance 60 m; displacement 60 m, as both measure her walk
Distance 60 m; displacement 30 m, the furthest point reached
Distance 30 m; displacement 30 m west, using the return leg

items.why: Distance is measured along the whole path walked, 30 m + 30 m = 60 m. The straight line from start point to finish point has no length, so the displacement is zero.

items.stem: A walker sets off from a car park, goes 3.0 km due east and then 4.0 km due north. Which of these correctly expresses her displacement from the car park?

options.text: 7.0 km, on a heading 37 degrees east of north
5.0 km, in a direction 37 degrees east of north
5.0 km, and no direction needs to be stated
1.0 km, due north of the car park she left

items.why: The two legs are at right angles, so the magnitude is the square root of (3.0^2 + 4.0^2) = 5.0 km, and a displacement must also carry the direction of that straight line.

items.stem: Two cars travel along the same straight road at 20 m/s, one heading north and the other heading south. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Their speeds are equal but their velocities differ
Their speeds and their velocities are both equal
Their speeds differ, but their velocities match
Neither their speeds nor velocities are equal

items.why: Speed is a scalar, so both are 20 m/s. Velocity is speed in a given direction, and the directions are opposite, so the velocities differ.

items.stem: A student sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 6.0 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, how far away was the lightning?
items.why: Using distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t = 330 m/s × 6.0 s = 1980 m.

items.stem: A train travels at a constant speed of 45 m/s. How long does it take to travel 9.0 km?
items.why: Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Converting 9.0 km to 9000 m, t = 9000 / 45 = 200 s.

items.stem: A student wants to measure the average speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp. Which method should she use?

options.text: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then multiply these
Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then divide distance by time
Measure the distance and the time, then divide the time by the distance
Measure the time for the trip twice and then find the mean of them

items.why: Speed is found by making measurements of distance and of time and then dividing the distance by the time taken.

items.stem: A car's speed changes constantly during a journey through town. How should its average speed for the journey be found?

options.text: Add together the highest and the lowest speeds, then halve that
Divide the total time taken by the total distance moved
Divide the total distance travelled by the total time taken
Read the speedometer at the halfway point of the trip

items.why: Average speed for non-uniform motion is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stopped.

items.stem: A cyclist rides 4.0 km in 500 s, rests for 100 s, and then rides 5.0 km in 400 s. What is her average speed for the whole journey?

options.text: 10 m/s
8 m/s

items.why: Total distance is 9000 m and total time is 1000 s, so the average speed is 9000 / 1000 = 9.0 m/s.

items.stem: On a distance-time graph a straight line passes through the origin and through the point (8.0 s, 120 m). What is the speed of the object?

options.text: 15 m/s
8 m/s

items.why: The gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time: 120 m / 8.0 s = 15 m/s.

items.stem: Part of a distance-time graph for a car is a horizontal straight line. What is the car doing during that part?

options.text: It is moving at a steady speed there
It is stationary and staying put
It is going back towards the start
It is speeding up all the time

items.why: A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the distance is not changing and the speed is zero.

items.stem: The distance-time graph for an accelerating car is a curve. How should the speed of the car at 6 s be found?

options.text: Join the origin to the point at 6 s and find that gradient
Read the distance at 6 s straight off the vertical axis
Draw a tangent to the curve at 6 s and measure its gradient
Find the area under the curve up to the 6 s point

items.why: For an accelerating object the speed at a particular time is the gradient of the tangent drawn to the distance-time graph at that time.

items.stem: On a distance-time graph the line curves upwards and becomes steeper as time goes on. What does this show?

options.text: The object is slowing down as time goes on
The object moves at a steady high speed
The object is moving away from the start
The object is speeding up as time goes on

items.why: An increasing gradient means the distance covered each second is growing, so the object is speeding up.

items.stem: A motorbike speeds up from 5 m/s to 29 m/s in 6.0 s. What is its average acceleration?

options.text: 24 m/s

items.why: Using a = (change in velocity) / t, the change in velocity is 29 - 5 = 24 m/s, so a = 24 / 6.0 = 4 m/s^2.

items.stem: A train slows down uniformly from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 40 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is now travelling backwards along the track at 10 m/s
It is decelerating, and so its acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2
It is decelerating at 0.25 m/s^2, from 10 m/s in 40 s
It is accelerating at 0.5 m/s^2 along the track

items.why: An object that slows down is decelerating. The change in velocity is -20 m/s in 40 s, so the acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2.

items.stem: Which is the best estimate of the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights?

options.text: About 100 m/s^2, so reaching 12 m/s in around 0.1 s
About 9.8 m/s^2, the same as an object falling
About 2 m/s^2, reaching some 12 m/s in about 6 s
About 0.02 m/s^2, reaching 12 m/s in 10 min

items.why: A sensible everyday estimate: 2 m/s^2 sustained for 6 s gives 12 m/s, a reasonable town speed.

items.stem: A velocity-time graph for a cyclist is a straight line rising from 0 m/s to 15 m/s over 8.0 s. What distance does the cyclist travel in that time?
items.why: The distance is the area under the line, a triangle: 0.5 × 8.0 s × 15 m/s = 60 m.

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly at 3.5 m/s^2 from an initial velocity of 24 m/s over a distance of 7.0 m. What is its final velocity?

options.text: 25 m/s
7 m/s

items.stem: (Higher tier) What is meant by the inertia of an object?

options.text: A forward force that keeps a moving object going.
A property that increases as an object moves faster.
The resistance of the air to an object moving through it.
Its tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.

items.why: Inertia is exactly the tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.

items.stem: The resultant force acting on a trolley is doubled while its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration of the trolley?

options.text: Its speed doubles, but the acceleration stays as it was.
It halves, because the force has more work to do now.
It doubles, as acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
It is unchanged, since the trolley's mass is the same.

items.why: Newton's Second Law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, so twice the force gives twice the acceleration.

items.stem: The mass of a trolley is trebled while the resultant force acting on it is kept the same. What happens to its acceleration?

options.text: It trebles, because the trolley is three times heavier.
It stays the same, since the force is unchanged.
It falls to a ninth of the value it had before.
The acceleration falls to a third of its old value.

items.why: Acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass of the object, so three times the mass under the same resultant force gives one third of the acceleration.

items.stem: In the equation resultant force = mass x acceleration, which set of units must be used?

options.text: force in newtons, N; mass in kilograms, kg; acceleration in m/s
force in newtons, N; mass in grams, g; acceleration in m/s^2
force in kilograms, mass in newtons, acceleration in m/s^2
force in newtons, N; mass in kilograms, kg; acceleration in m/s^2

items.why: The specification gives force, F, in newtons, N; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; and acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2.

items.stem: Why is acceleration measured in metres per second squared, m/s^2?

options.text: A change of velocity in m/s is divided by a time in s.
A distance in metres is divided by a time in seconds twice.
A velocity in m/s is multiplied by the time taken.
The object covers a squared distance each second.

items.why: Acceleration is a velocity change divided by the time it takes, so its unit is m/s divided by s, which is written m/s^2.

items.stem: (Higher tier) What does the inertial mass of an object measure?

options.text: The size of the gravitational pull acting on the object.
How difficult it is to change the object's velocity.
How fast the object is able to travel once it is released.
The force needed to keep the object still on Earth.

items.why: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object.

items.stem: (Higher tier) How is inertial mass defined?

options.text: As the acceleration divided by the force.
As the weight of the object divided by 10 N/kg.
As the ratio of force over acceleration.
As the force multiplied by the acceleration.

items.why: The specification defines inertial mass as the ratio of force over acceleration, matching m = F / a from F = m a.

items.stem: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 3000 N' at the end of an estimate. What does the symbol ~ tell the reader?

options.text: The force is smaller than 3000 N at every moment.
The force is at most 3000 N, never any higher.
The 3000 N is an approximate value, not an exact one.
The force changes in size as the car speeds up on the road.

items.why: The symbol indicates an approximate value or approximate answer, which is what an estimate from rounded data produces.

items.stem: A crate rests on a level floor. Its weight is 400 N downwards and the floor pushes upwards on it with a force of 400 N. Which statement about the crate is correct?

options.text: The resultant force on the crate is zero, so it stays stationary.
No force at all acts on the crate while it is not moving.
The crate's weight and the floor's push are a third law pair.
The two forces add up to 800 N pressing on the floor.

items.why: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero, and a stationary object with zero resultant force remains stationary.

items.stem: A puck slides in a straight line across a level ice rink at a steady 4 m/s. Friction and air resistance are so small that they can be ignored. What is the resultant force on the puck?

options.text: It acts forwards, because the puck is still moving forwards.
It is zero, because the puck's velocity is not changing.
It acts backwards, so the puck is very slowly stopping.
It is 4 N forwards, matching the puck's steady speed.

items.why: The speed and the direction are both constant, so the velocity is constant, and by Newton's First Law the resultant force must be zero.

items.stem: A van travels along a straight level road at a steady 25 m/s. The driving force from its engine is 900 N. What can be said about the resistive forces on the van?

options.text: They are smaller than 900 N, which is why the van moves.
They are larger than 900 N, so the van is losing speed.
They total 900 N, acting backwards along the road.
They are zero, as the road surface is smooth.

items.why: At a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force, so together they come to 900 N in the opposite direction.

items.stem: A skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity before opening her parachute. Which statement explains her motion?

options.text: Her weight has fallen to zero, so nothing is pulling her downwards.
Her weight and the air resistance are equal, so the resultant is zero.
The air resistance is now larger than her weight as she falls.
A downward resultant force keeps her moving downwards at speed.

items.why: A constant velocity means a zero resultant force, which here means the upward air resistance has grown until it balances her downward weight exactly.

items.stem: A book lies at rest on a table. Which statement about the forces on the book is correct?

options.text: There are no forces on the book while it lies still.
The table's push must be bigger, to hold the book up.
Its weight and the table's push give a resultant of zero.
The book's weight is bigger, but the table is far too solid.

items.why: Two forces act on the book, downward weight and the table's upward push; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant force on the book is zero.

items.stem: (Higher tier) A bus brakes sharply and the standing passengers lurch forwards. Why does this happen?

options.text: They keep moving at their original velocity.
A forward force throws them out of their places.
Their inertia acts as a forward push on their bodies.
The braking force acts on the bus and then on them.

items.why: Inertia: with no resultant backward force on them, the passengers continue in their state of uniform motion while the bus slows beneath them.

items.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a resultant force acting on it that gives it an acceleration of 2.5 m/s^2. What is the size of that resultant force?
items.why: resultant force = mass x acceleration, so F = 1200 kg x 2.5 m/s^2 = 3000 N.

items.stem: A go-kart and driver of total mass 500 kg have a driving force of 2500 N acting forwards on them and resistive forces of 500 N acting backwards. What is the acceleration?
items.why: The resultant force is 2500 N - 500 N = 2000 N, so a = F / m = 2000 N / 500 kg = 4 m/s^2.

items.stem: A family car reaches a speed of about 27 m/s from rest in about 9 s. Estimate its acceleration.

options.text: ~3 m/s^2, from a gain of about 27 m/s in about 9 s
~27 m/s^2, the speed the car reaches on the road
~240 m/s^2, from 27 m/s multiplied by the 9 s
~9 m/s^2, the same as free fall near the Earth

items.why: Dividing the change of velocity by the time gives 27 / 9 = 3, so the acceleration is about 3 m/s^2, quoted as an approximate value.

items.stem: A car of mass about 1000 kg accelerates at about 3 m/s^2. Estimate the resultant force acting on it.

options.text: ~330 N, from 1000 kg divided by 3 m/s^2
~3000 N, from 1000 kg multiplied by 3 m/s^2
~10 000 N, which is the weight of the car itself
~3 N, as the acceleration is about 3 m/s^2

items.why: resultant force = mass x acceleration, so the estimate is about 1000 x 3 = 3000 N, a force of a few thousand newtons.

items.stem: In required practical activity 7, a trolley is pulled along a bench by masses hanging on a string over a pulley. When investigating how the force affects the acceleration, what must be kept constant?

options.text: The load left on the trolley.
The acceleration of the loaded trolley.
The speed of the trolley at each gate.
The total mass being accelerated.

items.why: The investigation varies the force on an object of constant mass, so masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger and the total accelerating mass is unchanged.

items.stem: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with a force of 200 N. What force does the water exert on the swimmer?

options.text: Less than 200 N, because water is pushed aside so easily.
400 N forwards, twice as large as the swimmer's push.
200 N forwards, equal in size and opposite to her push.
200 N backwards, in the same direction as her push.

items.why: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite, so the water pushes forwards on the swimmer with 200 N.

items.stem: A car is driven all the way round a roundabout at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Is there a resultant force acting on the car?

options.text: No, since the speed stays at a steady 10 m/s.
No, the forces on the car must all be balanced.
Only if the driver presses the brake pedal.
Yes, because its direction is changing.

items.why: Velocity is speed and direction. The direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes, and velocity only changes if a resultant force acts.

items.stem: In the second part of required practical activity 7 the pulling force is kept constant and extra masses are placed on the trolley. What happens to the measured acceleration?

options.text: It stays the same, as the pulling force has not changed.
It falls, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
It rises, since a heavier trolley carries more force with it.
It falls to a quarter each time the mass is doubled.

items.why: With a constant resultant force, a = F / m, so adding mass lowers the acceleration and a graph of acceleration against mass curves downwards.

items.stem: A book rests in equilibrium on a table. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?

options.text: The weight of the book and the upward push of the table on the book.
The weight of the book and the friction between it and the table.
The table's push up and the floor's push up on the table.
The book's push down on the table and the table's push up on it.

items.why: A third law pair is the two forces two interacting objects exert on each other: here the book on the table and the table on the book, equal and opposite.

items.stem: A horse pulls a cart forwards. The cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why does the cart still accelerate?

options.text: The two forces act on different objects.
Because the horse is far stronger than the cart is.
It does not, so the loaded cart can never move.
The horse's pull comes a moment before the cart's.

items.why: A third law pair never cancels, because only forces acting on the same object can be added; the cart accelerates because of the forces acting on the cart alone.
